analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the ban on exporting American crude oil and natural gas, keeping those fuels at home.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2018 with two cosponsors, the bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring back the ban on shipping American crude oil and natural gas to foreign buyers, a ban Congress had lifted in 2015. It would require the President to write a rule prohibiting those exports, while allowing exemptions if the President decides an export serves the national interest. It also gives the President optional authority to restrict exports of coal, refined petroleum products, petrochemical feedstocks, and even energy equipment and materials.
analysis.who_benefits: American households that buy gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas. The bill's premise is that fuel produced in the United States should stay in the United States, so domestic supply is not bid up by foreign buyers. Refineries that rely on domestic crude could also benefit from guaranteed access to domestic oil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US consumers of gasoline and natural gas

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require the President to issue a rule prohibiting the export of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, with exemptions only where the President finds the export consistent with the national interest [S2][S3].

It also gives the President authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and petrochemical feedstocks, and of materials and equipment needed for domestic energy production, refining, and facilities [S3].
The President must still account for historical trade with Canada and Mexico and cross-border transport conveniences when imposing restrictions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers and exporters, who lose access to foreign markets for US crude and gas, and companies that invested in export terminals and shipping on the expectation that the 2015 repeal was permanent. If restricting exports dampens production, oilfield workers and communities could see reduced drilling activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

drawbacks.text: Most economic studies at the time of the 2015 repeal projected that allowing exports would actually lower US gasoline prices, by encouraging more domestic production and more efficient refining, so a ban could raise rather than lower costs for consumers (general knowledge about the export-ban debate).

The bill hands the President sweeping, discretionary power to restrict exports of coal, gas, petroleum products, and energy equipment by rule, and even to waive the usual public notice-and-comment process, without requiring any declared emergency [S3].
A broad export ban invites trade retaliation from countries that buy American energy, which could hit other US export industries (general knowledge about trade policy).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill rests on a contested premise: that keeping crude and gas at home lowers US energy prices. Supporters like Senator Markey argued exports send domestically produced fuel abroad and push up what Americans pay; industry-backed analyses at the time of the 2015 repeal found the opposite, crediting exports with boosting production and lowering gasoline prices. The bill also grants the executive very broad export-control power over coal and other goods beyond the crude-and-gas ban, which is a real structural concern regardless of where one lands on energy prices. On balance, the bill pursues a defensible consumer-protection goal with a blunt tool whose main documented effect would fall on producers and exporters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 21, 2018; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
Two Democratic senators cosponsored it, and the bill received no further committee or floor action before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

The export ban the bill sought to reinstate had been lifted by Congress in the 2015 Consolidated Appropriations Act, which the bill would partially roll back by striking key provisions of that law [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and exporters, who kept unrestricted access to foreign markets for American crude and natural gas; the law remained exactly as they preferred it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the crude oil and natural gas export ban and referred it to the Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: US oil and gas industry
against.role: Exporters of domestic crude and natural gas
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating the export ban, which would cut off foreign markets for domestic crude and gas, after having backed the 2015 repeal that opened them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and it died in a Republican-run Senate without ever reaching a vote, so the small amount of support was entirely from one party.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill would bar exporting US crude oil and natural gas, cutting these companies off from foreign buyers who currently pay for roughly millions of barrels of American oil. Their interest in keeping export markets open runs against the bill's aim of holding fuel supply at home for US consumers.

The bill gives the President optional authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, and petrochemical feedstocks, creating a risk these exporters cannot fully plan around. Unlike the crude-and-gas ban, this is discretionary rather than mandatory.

industries.industry: Liquefied natural gas terminal and shipping investors
industries.note: A prohibition on natural gas exports would undercut terminals and shipping capacity built after the 2015 repeal on the expectation of permanent access to foreign markets.
